title: Will you ever be good?
hook: will you ever be simple, whole, unconcealed? (Meditations 10.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was pray differently: not only let this pass, but let me not fear it. Your line was let me not fear.

A face for work. A face for family dinners. A face for the group chat. Each one fits, and each can be a little tiring to wear. Underneath them all, someone is doing the switching. Book ten of the Meditations opens with Marcus asking about that someone, not as a theory, but in the second person, like someone gently shaking his own shoulder.
screen: `A FACE FOR EVERY ROOM.` → `WHO'S UNDERNEATH?` → `BOOK TEN OPENS.`

segments.voice: Marcus speaks to his own soul: will you ever, my soul, be good and simple and one and naked, plainer to see than the body that surrounds you? It isn't a rule. It's a question he doesn't know the answer to. Take the words. Good. Simple: single, one fold, not doubled over. One: whole, not split into different pieces for different rooms. Naked: unconcealed, nothing hidden under the surface that would contradict what shows. And the questions keep coming. Will you ever, he asks, taste a loving and contented disposition? Be full, needing nothing, craving nothing, not wanting more time to enjoy pleasures, or a better place, or nicer weather, or better company? Will you be satisfied with what's here, and believe that all is well with you? Why this matters on a Tuesday: some tiredness may not come from the work at all, but from the switching, minding the gap between the person inside and the one we're presenting. Marcus wants to close that gap. Not by telling everyone everything; simple doesn't mean blurting. It means there's one person in there, the same in every room. And notice how he asks: as a question, to himself, with no answer written down.
screen: `MY SOUL, WILL YOU EVER?` · `GOOD, SIMPLE, ONE, UNCONCEALED.` · `FULL, NEEDING NOTHING.` · `ONE PERSON IN EVERY ROOM.` · then, large: `SIMPLE AND WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Think of a room in your life where you wear the heaviest face: a meeting, a family visit, a feed. Notice what you trim away there, not secrets that belong to other people, just parts of yourself. Choose one small, true thing you could let show, a real opinion kindly said, a real feeling, a plain no, and breathe with it.
Contented disposition. Marcus asks his soul whether it will ever taste a loving and contented disposition, satisfied with what's here. Today's word.
Your line: simple and whole. Good, simple, one, unconcealed, the same in every room. That's day six hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations sometimes use Marcus's opening question in book ten as an honest self-check, asking where they present a different self in different rooms, and choosing one place to be plainer.
